doc.title: Al Grey interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995

title: Navy boot camp at Great Lakes: tuba and bugle corps
summary: Grey, finishing Pottstown High School, joins the Navy at Great Lakes. He plays tuba, joins the bugle and drum corps and attends football games.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Well that’d be wonderful. I start back in the United States Navy. And as you know it was a long time before the blacks could enter the United States Navy, and when this came about I was still in school and I says well I know they’re getting ready to draft me into the Army so before they draft me into the Army I will shoot for the Navy. So coming out of the of the Pottstown High School, in which I had played all the marches and played with the school dance band, but I played tuba, see. Because we didn’t have any money and this is what the school had to offer, and they said the opportunity is to play the tuba. And so this was not the B flat tuba, the E flat tuba, which is different fingering from the regular bass clef instrument. And so I go out to Great Lakes, Illinois, where they had all these great musicians from all the great famous bands. And that was like musicians from Basie, Cab Calloway, Ellington, Les Brown, Jimmie Lunceford, and all these musicians was out there. So many musicians that they had to send musicians off to the various different camps, you know? And I entered into boot camp but I wanted to play music so I joined a bugle and drum corps. So I played the bugle. And in the morning I’d get up and play the colors, and learned all those different calls, but the glory and happiness of that ©Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

was that when the Great Lakes football team would play, you’d have that privilege of going to the games with the bugle and drum corps, see? And that was a treat because that’s where they had Otto and Martin Graham and all those great football players that had come out of the various different schools. And from there I would try to play trombone because the tuba had become obsolete, where the tuba had went out. There was no more tuba playing in which it’s coming back today again. It’s that cycle going around.
